description: Design system regulations for health and medical applications, encompassing HIPAA compliance, FDA guidelines, clinical safety requirements, WCAG accessibility, and patient-centered design principles.

references.name: HIPAA Privacy Rule
references.description: Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act requirements for protecting patient health information.

references.name: FDA Mobile Medical Applications Guidance
references.description: FDA guidance on the regulation of mobile medical applications.

references.name: WCAG 2.1 Level AA
references.description: Web Content Accessibility Guidelines, especially important for health applications serving diverse populations.

references.name: IEC 62366 Usability Engineering
references.description: International standard for usability engineering of medical devices.

references.name: Section 508
references.description: Federal accessibility requirements applicable to health IT systems.

regulations.title: HIPAA UI Compliance
regulations.description: User interfaces must enforce HIPAA requirements for the display, transmission, and storage of Protected Health Information (PHI).

rules.requirement: PHI must be masked or hidden by default on screen. Users must perform an explicit action (tap to reveal, authentication) to view full PHI. Partial masking (showing last 4 digits of MRN) is acceptable for identification.
rules.rationale: PHI displayed openly on screen can be exposed through shoulder surfing, screen sharing, or screenshots.

rules.requirement: Applications must display a visible countdown or warning at least 30 seconds before an automatic session timeout occurs, giving users the option to extend their session.
rules.rationale: Healthcare professionals need time to save work before HIPAA-mandated session expiration.

rules.requirement: Applications must provide a user-accessible audit log showing who accessed a patient record and when, meeting HIPAA's minimum necessary standard.
rules.rationale: HIPAA requires accounting of disclosures and access auditing for PHI.

rules.requirement: Screens displaying PHI must prevent or warn about screen capture. On mobile, FLAG_SECURE (Android) or screen recording notifications (iOS) must be implemented.
rules.rationale: Screen captures of PHI create unencrypted copies that violate HIPAA safeguards.

regulations.title: Clinical Safety UI Standards
regulations.description: User interfaces for clinical workflows must minimize the risk of patient harm through clear, unambiguous design.

rules.requirement: Abnormal or critical lab values, vital signs, and medication alerts must be visually distinct using both color and iconography (e.g., red background plus warning icon). Critical values must use a minimum text size of 18sp/pt.
rules.rationale: Missed critical values can lead to delayed treatment and patient harm.

rules.requirement: Medication names must use Tall Man lettering (e.g., DOBUTamine vs DOPamine) to differentiate look-alike/sound-alike (LASA) drug names. Generic and brand names must both be displayed.
rules.rationale: ISMP and FDA recommend Tall Man lettering to reduce medication errors from name confusion.

rules.requirement: Dosage input fields must enforce range limits, display the unit of measurement alongside the input, and require explicit confirmation for values exceeding typical ranges.
rules.rationale: Incorrect dosage entry is a leading cause of medication errors in health IT systems.

rules.requirement: Irreversible clinical actions (medication administration, order signing, discharge) must require a two-step confirmation with a clear summary of the action being taken.
rules.rationale: Single-tap irreversible actions in clinical contexts can result in patient safety incidents.

rules.requirement: Every clinical screen must display at least two patient identifiers (name plus date of birth, or name plus MRN) in a fixed, prominent location to prevent wrong-patient errors.
rules.rationale: The Joint Commission's National Patient Safety Goals require two-identifier verification.

regulations.title: Health Application Accessibility
regulations.description: Health applications must exceed standard accessibility requirements due to the critical nature of health information and the diverse needs of patient populations.

rules.requirement: Text contrast must meet WCAG 2.1 Level AAA (7:1 for normal text, 4.5:1 for large text) for all clinical data displays.
rules.rationale: Clinical environments often have suboptimal lighting, and users may have impaired vision.

rules.requirement: Clinical data text (vitals, lab results, medication names) must be at least 16sp/pt at default scale and must support user scaling up to 300%.
rules.rationale: Healthcare workers may read screens at a distance or under stress; larger text reduces errors.

rules.requirement: All clinical data must be properly structured for screen readers with logical grouping, meaningful labels, and correct reading order. Tabular data must use proper table semantics.
rules.rationale: Healthcare professionals and patients with visual impairments must be able to access health data.

rules.requirement: Patient-facing health applications must support at minimum English and Spanish, with the ability to add additional languages. Medical terminology must be available in plain language.
rules.rationale: Limited English proficiency is a significant barrier to healthcare access in the US.

rules.requirement: Health information must be presented at a maximum 6th-grade reading level for patient-facing content. Medical jargon must be supplemented with plain-language explanations.
rules.rationale: Average US health literacy is at the 7th-8th grade level; targeting 6th grade ensures broader comprehension.

regulations.title: Clinical Data Visualization
regulations.description: Clinical data must be presented in clear, accurate, and standardized formats to support safe clinical decision-making.

rules.requirement: Vital signs must display the value, unit of measurement, timestamp, and reference range. Values outside the reference range must be visually flagged.
rules.rationale: Complete vital sign context is essential for clinical decision-making.

rules.requirement: Lab results must include the test name, value, unit, reference range, and flag (high/low/critical). Historical trends must be accessible via a chart or table view.
rules.rationale: Incomplete lab data can lead to misinterpretation and inappropriate clinical decisions.

rules.requirement: All clinical timestamps must display date, time, and timezone. The format must be unambiguous (e.g., 13 Apr 2026, 14:30 EDT). Relative times (e.g., '2 hours ago') must not be used for clinical data.
rules.rationale: Ambiguous timestamps in clinical contexts can lead to timing errors in care delivery.

rules.requirement: Clinical charts must include labeled axes with units, a legend when multiple data series are shown, and interactive data point inspection. Y-axis must start at a clinically meaningful zero or baseline.
rules.rationale: Misleading charts can cause incorrect interpretation of patient trends.

regulations.title: Clinical Color System
regulations.description: Colors in health applications must follow clinical conventions and ensure safety-critical information is never conveyed by color alone.

rules.requirement: Red must be reserved exclusively for critical/life-threatening alerts and abnormal-high values. Yellow/amber for warnings. Green for normal/within-range values. These color assignments must not be repurposed for branding.
rules.rationale: Clinical staff associate red with emergencies; using red for branding causes alert confusion.

rules.requirement: Allergy alerts must use a distinct, high-contrast color scheme (e.g., red text on yellow/white background) that is unique within the application and not used for any other alert type.
rules.rationale: Allergy alerts must stand out to prevent potentially fatal allergic reactions from missed alerts.

rules.requirement: Clinical status colors must be distinguishable by users with protanopia, deuteranopia, and tritanopia. Simulated color-blind testing must be part of the design review process.
rules.rationale: Approximately 8% of male healthcare workers may have color vision deficiency.

rules.requirement: All color-coded clinical information must include a secondary visual indicator: icon, pattern, shape, or text label alongside the color.
rules.rationale: Color-only coding fails for color-blind users and in poor lighting conditions common in clinical settings.

regulations.title: Health Typography Standards
regulations.description: Typography in health applications must prioritize legibility and error reduction in high-stakes reading conditions.

rules.requirement: Fonts used for clinical data must clearly disambiguate easily confused characters: 0 (zero) vs O (letter), 1 (one) vs l (lowercase L) vs I (uppercase i). Tabular/monospaced numerals are required for data tables.
rules.rationale: Character confusion in clinical data (e.g., dosage amounts) can cause patient harm.

rules.requirement: Critical information must use bold or semibold weight rather than color or italics alone for emphasis. Italic text must not be used for warnings or critical values.
rules.rationale: Bold is more universally perceivable than color or italics across vision conditions.

rules.requirement: Clinical narrative text (physician notes, discharge summaries) must have a maximum line length of 80 characters to maintain readability.
rules.rationale: Long lines of medical text increase reading errors and decrease comprehension speed.

regulations.title: Clinical Interaction Patterns
regulations.description: Interaction patterns in health applications must prevent errors and support the high-pressure, time-constrained clinical workflow.

rules.requirement: Destructive actions (delete records, cancel orders) must require a distinct gesture from standard navigation. A confirmation dialog must clearly state what will be affected and the action must be undoable for at least 30 seconds when possible.
rules.rationale: In high-pressure clinical environments, accidental taps on destructive actions are common.

rules.requirement: Patient search must support search by name, MRN, date of birth, and partial matching. Results must display enough identifying information to prevent wrong-patient selection.
rules.rationale: Efficient, unambiguous patient search is critical to preventing wrong-patient errors.

rules.requirement: Clinical documentation entry (notes, assessments, orders) must auto-save drafts at least every 60 seconds with visual indication of save status.
rules.rationale: Healthcare workers are frequently interrupted; lost documentation wastes time and delays care.

rules.requirement: Barcode/QR code scanning for medication and patient identification must provide clear visual framing, real-time feedback on scan success or failure, and a manual entry fallback.
rules.rationale: Barcode scanning is a critical safety verification step; failures must not block the workflow.

regulations.title: Patient Data Privacy UI
regulations.description: User interface design must enforce patient data privacy requirements beyond basic HIPAA compliance.

rules.requirement: Accessing restricted patient records must present a prominent 'break-the-glass' confirmation screen requiring reason documentation before granting access.
rules.rationale: Break-the-glass auditing is a HIPAA requirement for access to restricted records.

rules.requirement: Patient consent status for data sharing, research participation, and advance directives must be clearly displayed with effective dates and source documentation links.
rules.rationale: Clinical decisions depend on current consent status; unclear display leads to compliance violations.

rules.requirement: Screens must display only the minimum PHI necessary for the user's role and current task. Role-based field-level visibility must be enforced in the UI.
rules.rationale: HIPAA's minimum necessary standard requires limiting PHI exposure to what is needed.

regulations.title: Clinical Component Standards
regulations.description: Specialized UI components for health applications must follow clinical conventions and safety standards.

rules.requirement: Medication list components must display drug name (generic + brand), dose, route, frequency, prescriber, and status. Active medications must be visually separated from discontinued or historical medications.
rules.rationale: Complete, organized medication lists reduce prescribing errors and drug interactions.

rules.requirement: Clinical alert banners must be persistent (not auto-dismissing), color-coded by severity, and include an action button. Critical alerts must require explicit acknowledgment before dismissal.
rules.rationale: Auto-dismissing clinical alerts can be missed, leading to patient safety events.

rules.requirement: A persistent patient header must be visible on all clinical screens showing: patient name, photo (if available), age, sex, MRN, and active allergy count with severity indicator.
rules.rationale: Constant patient context prevents wrong-patient actions across screen transitions.

regulations.title: Clinical Layout Standards
regulations.description: Screen layouts in health applications must support efficient clinical workflows and rapid information retrieval.

rules.requirement: Clinical screens must balance information density with readability. Summary views should display 5-7 key data points; detail views can show more but must use clear section grouping.
rules.rationale: Cognitive overload from excessive data points increases clinical error rates.

rules.requirement: Clinical screens must use consistent layout zones: patient header (top), alerts/notifications (below header), primary content (center), and actions (bottom). This arrangement must remain consistent across all clinical screens.
rules.rationale: Consistent layout zones reduce cognitive load and speed up information finding.

rules.requirement: Clinical applications on tablet devices must support split-view layouts allowing side-by-side display of patient lists and individual records.
rules.rationale: Clinical workflows often require comparing data across views simultaneously.
